why: Generate permutations of 1..n by backtracking, but only append a value whose parity differs from the last value placed. Trying values in increasing order at every position emits the permutations already in lexicographic order, so no sorting is needed.
hints: This is 'all permutations' with one extra rule between neighbours. Where can you enforce the rule so bad branches are never explored?
When choosing the next value, skip any used value and any value with the same parity as the current last element. Try values from small to large.
Backtrack with a used[] array and a current list; on length n, copy it into the result. The output itself is the cost (about (n/2)!^2 permutations), so keep the per-node work O(n).
pitfalls: Order is numeric lexicographic (10 > 9), not string order.
For odd n, sequences must start and end with an odd number; the pruning handles this automatically, but a parity-counting shortcut must respect it.
constraints: • 1 <= n (no upper bound is stated in the source; since the output grows like ((n/2)!)^2, expect n to be about 10 or less).
